entries.english: to be / am / is / are
entries.shortExplanation: N이에요 / 예요 means "to be / am / is / are" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: N이에요 / 예요 (N-ieyo / yeyo) means "to be / am / is / are" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 학생이에요 ("I am a student."). Use 이에요 after a final consonant and 예요 after a vowel.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize two complete polite examples. Then substitute one word at a time and check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective.
entries.contextHint: Use this for identity, names, jobs, places, and simple “it is...” sentences. It does not describe actions.

patternInfo.meaning: to be / am / is / are
patternInfo.formNote: Use 이에요 after a final consonant and 예요 after a vowel.

studyGuide.title: Noun sentences
howToBuild: Choose a noun.
Use 이에요 after a final consonant and 예요 after a vowel.
Use 입니다 when the situation is very formal.
studyGuide.whenToUse: Use this for identity, names, jobs, places, and simple “it is...” sentences. It does not describe actions.
studyGuide.learnerPath: After this, study 있어요 and 없어요 so you can say what something is and whether it exists.

examples.en: I am a student.
This place is a school.
My name is Hana.

entries.nuance: Use 이에요 after a final consonant and 예요 after a vowel.

entries.english: there is / have
entries.shortExplanation: N이/가 있어요 means "there is / have" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "there is / have" uses the pattern N이/가 있어요 (N-i/ga isseoyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 시간이 있어요 ("I have time."). Use for existence or possession. 이 follows consonants; 가 follows vowels.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize two complete polite examples. Then substitute one word at a time and check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective.
entries.contextHint: Use it for having time, money, reservations, friends, or for asking whether something exists in a place.

patternInfo.meaning: there is / have
patternInfo.formNote: Use for existence or possession. 이 follows consonants; 가 follows vowels.

studyGuide.title: Existence and possession
howToBuild: Put the thing before 이/가.
Use 이 after a consonant and 가 after a vowel.
Add 있어요 for “there is” or “I have.”
studyGuide.whenToUse: Use it for having time, money, reservations, friends, or for asking whether something exists in a place.
studyGuide.learnerPath: Pair this with 없어요. Together they cover many beginner travel and classroom situations.

examples.en: I have time.
Is there a bathroom here?
I have a reservation.

entries.english: there is not / do not have

entries.explanation: N이/가 없어요 (N-i/ga eopseoyo) = "there is not / do not have". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 시간이 없어요 ("I do not have time."). Use for absence or not having something.

studyGuide.learnerPath: This is different from V아/어 주세요. N 주세요 asks for a thing; V아/어 주세요 asks someone to do an action.

entries.english: cannot / be unable to
entries.shortExplanation: 못 + verb means "cannot / be unable to" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "cannot / be unable to" uses the pattern 못 + verb (mot + verb). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 못 가요 ("I cannot go."). For most verbs, put 못 before the normal verb form: 가요 becomes 못 가요. For 하다 verbs, use 못 해요 or noun 못 해요. Never make forms like 못 가해요.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize two complete polite examples. Then substitute one word at a time and check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective.
entries.contextHint: Use it for inability, schedule conflicts, food restrictions, or language limits: 못 가요, 못 먹어요, 한국어를 잘 못해요. It says “I cannot” because of a real limit, not simply “I choose not to.”

patternInfo.meaning: cannot / be unable to
patternInfo.formNote: For most verbs, put 못 before the normal verb form: 가요 becomes 못 가요. For 하다 verbs, use 못 해요 or noun 못 해요. Never make forms like 못 가해요.

studyGuide.title: Cannot / unable to
howToBuild: For most verbs, put 못 before the normal polite verb: 가요 becomes 못 가요, 먹어요 becomes 못 먹어요.
Do not add 해요 to a non-하다 verb. It is 못 가요, not 못 가해요.
For 하다 verbs, use 못 해요 or noun 못 해요: 해요 becomes 못 해요, 공부해요 becomes 공부 못 해요.
studyGuide.whenToUse: Use it for inability, schedule conflicts, food restrictions, or language limits: 못 가요, 못 먹어요, 한국어를 잘 못해요. It says “I cannot” because of a real limit, not simply “I choose not to.”
studyGuide.learnerPath: This is a survival pattern. First memorize real examples like 못 가요, 못 먹어요, and 말 못 해요 before trying to build new ones.

examples.en: I cannot go today.

entries.shortExplanation: V아서/어서 means "because / so" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V아서/어서 (V-aseo/eoseo) = "because / so". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 바빠서 못 가요 ("I am busy, so I cannot go."). Connect a reason to a result. Do not use it for commands or suggestions in formal grammar.

entries.contextHint: Use it to explain why something happened: 바빠서 못 가요, 아파서 쉬어요, 늦어서 죄송합니다. It lets beginners connect a reason to a result without making two separate sentences.

entries.english: you know (shared/obvious reason)
entries.shortExplanation: V/A-잖아요 means "you know (shared/obvious reason)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V/A-잖아요 (-janayo) = "you know (shared/obvious reason)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 내가 어제 말했잖아. ("I told you yesterday, remember."). Attach 잖아요 straight onto a plain verb or adjective stem; for past tense use 았/었잖아요. It reminds the listener of something you both already know, so it can sound a bit blaming if overused. There is no truly formal 합니다-style version, so reserve it for casual and 요 speech.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize two complete polite examples. Then substitute one word at a time and check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective.
entries.contextHint: Attach 잖아요 straight onto a plain verb or adjective stem; for past tense use 았/었잖아요. It reminds the listener of something you both already know, so it can sound a bit blaming if overused. There is no truly formal 합니다-style version, so reserve it for casual and 요 speech.

entries.nuance: Attach 잖아요 straight onto a plain verb or adjective stem; for past tense use 았/었잖아요. It reminds the listener of something you both already know, so it can sound a bit blaming if overused. There is no truly formal 합니다-style version, so reserve it for casual and 요 speech.

Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 저 오늘 못 가요. 약속이 있거든요. ("I can't come today. I have plans, see."). Add 거든요 to a plain verb or adjective stem to give a reason or background the listener doesn't know yet; for past use 았/었거든요. It often answers a 왜? or sets up a story, and the 요 keeps it polite. Said flatly to a stranger it can sound slightly defensive, so mind your tone.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize two complete polite examples. Then substitute one word at a time and check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective.

entries.english: I noticed / it turned out (firsthand)
entries.shortExplanation: V/A-더라고요 means "I noticed / it turned out (firsthand)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "I noticed / it turned out (firsthand)" uses the pattern V/A-더라고요 (-deoragoyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 가 보니까 생각보다 좋더라고요. ("When I went, it was better than I thought."). Attach 더라고요 to a plain verb or adjective stem to report something you personally saw, felt, or realized in the past. Because it is your own discovery, you normally do not use it about your own feelings or actions you were already aware of. The 고 is often dropped in speech, giving the very casual 더라.

entries.english: shall we? / wanna? / will you?
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ래요? means "shall we? / wanna? / will you?" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-(으)ㄹ래요? (-(eu)llaeyo) = "shall we? / wanna? / will you?". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 커피 마실래? ("Wanna grab coffee?"). Add ㄹ래요 after a vowel stem and 을래요 after a consonant stem; ㄹ-final stems keep their ㄹ and just add 래요 with no 으 (놀다 to 놀래요). As a question it casually suggests doing something together or asks the listener's will. As a statement it states your own intention (저 갈래요 = I'll go / I wanna go).
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize two complete polite examples. Then substitute one word at a time and check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective.
entries.contextHint: Add ㄹ래요 after a vowel stem and 을래요 after a consonant stem; ㄹ-final stems keep their ㄹ and just add 래요 with no 으 (놀다 to 놀래요). As a question it casually suggests doing something together or asks the listener's will. As a statement it states your own intention (저 갈래요 = I'll go / I wanna go).

patternInfo.meaning: shall we? / wanna? / will you?
patternInfo.formNote: Add ㄹ래요 after a vowel stem and 을래요 after a consonant stem; ㄹ-final stems keep their ㄹ and just add 래요 with no 으 (놀다 to 놀래요). As a question it casually suggests doing something together or asks the listener's will. As a statement it states your own intention (저 갈래요 = I'll go / I wanna go).

examples.en: If you're free this weekend, wanna catch a movie?
Wanna order delivery for lunch together?
Wanna grab a drink today? Just one round, light.

As a question it casually suggests doing something together or asks the listener's will. As a statement it states your own intention (저 갈래요 = I'll go / I wanna go).
commonMistakes: Do not use ㄹ래요? to invite someone clearly above you; use 같이 가시겠어요? or 같이 가실래요? to soften it.
ㄹ-final stems take just 래요 with no 으, so 놀다 becomes 놀래요, never 놀을래요.

entries.english: soft contrast / leading-on ending
entries.shortExplanation: V/A-는데요 means "soft contrast / leading-on ending" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V/A-는데요 (-neundeyo) means "soft contrast / leading-on ending" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 지금 좀 바쁜데요. ("I'm kind of busy right now, though."). Verbs take 는데요; adjectives take ㄴ데요 after a vowel and 은데요 after a consonant (좋다 to 좋은데요). 있다/없다 and past tense use 는데요 (재밌었는데요). Ending a sentence on 는데요 softens it, hints at a 'but...', or invites the other person to respond.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize two complete polite examples. Then substitute one word at a time and check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective.
entries.contextHint: Verbs take 는데요; adjectives take ㄴ데요 after a vowel and 은데요 after a consonant (좋다 to 좋은데요). 있다/없다 and past tense use 는데요 (재밌었는데요). Ending a sentence on 는데요 softens it, hints at a 'but...', or invites the other person to respond.

entries.english: I'm planning to / I intend to
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)려고요 means "I'm planning to / I intend to" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "I'm planning to / I intend to" uses the pattern V-(으)려고요 (-(eu)ryeogoyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 저 일찍 자려고요. ("I'm planning to sleep early."). Add 려고요 after a vowel stem and 으려고요 after a consonant stem to state your own intention, often as a reply to 'what are you going to do?'. It's the shortened, conversational form of 려고 해요. Use it only about your own plans, not someone else's.

entries.english: seems like / I guess (from evidence)
entries.shortExplanation: V/A-나 봐요 means "seems like / I guess (from evidence)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V/A-나 봐요 (-na bwayo) means "seems like / I guess (from evidence)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 비 오나 봐요. ("Looks like it's raining."). Verbs and 있다/없다 take 나 봐요 (오나 봐요). Descriptive adjectives usually take ㄴ가/은가 봐요 (바쁜가 봐요, 좋은가 봐요), and nouns take 인가 봐요. It expresses a guess based on something you observed, so don't use it about your own clear feelings.

entries.english: almost (did but didn't)
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요 means "almost (did but didn't)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "almost (did but didn't)" uses the pattern V-(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요 (-(eu)l ppeonhaesseoyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 늦을 뻔했어요. ("I almost ran late."). Add ㄹ 뻔했어요 after a vowel stem and 을 뻔했어요 after a consonant stem; ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ. It describes something that nearly happened but did NOT, almost always a near-miss or close call. It is fixed in the past tense (했어요).
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize two complete polite examples. Then substitute one word at a time and check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective.

entries.english: to pretend / act as if
entries.shortExplanation: V/A-는 척하다 means "to pretend / act as if" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V/A-는 척하다 (-neun cheokada) = "to pretend / act as if". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 자는 척했어. ("I pretended to be asleep."). Verbs take 는 척하다 (자는 척해요); adjectives take ㄴ/은 척하다 (예쁜 척해요, 괜찮은 척해요); past actions take 은/ㄴ 척하다 (안 들은 척해요). It means putting on an act you don't really feel or do. 척 can be swapped for the slightly more casual 체.

entries.shortExplanation: A/V-는 것 같아요 means "I think / it seems / it looks like (a softened guess or opinion)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.

entries.english: decided to / made up my mind to (often a plan or promise)
entries.shortExplanation: V-기로 했어요 means "decided to / made up my mind to (often a plan or promise)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "decided to / made up my mind to (often a plan or promise)" uses the pattern V-기로 했어요 (-giro haesseoyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 담배 끊기로 했어요 ("I decided to quit smoking"). Attach -기로 하다 directly to any verb stem with no sound change (운동하다 → 운동하기로, 끊다 → 끊기로). The decision is reported in the past tense (했어요) because the deciding already happened. Negative: V-지 않기로 했어요 or V-기로 안 했어요 (the first is more natural).

entries.english: ended up (completely) doing it — finished it off, often with regret or relief
entries.shortExplanation: V-아/어 버렸어요 means "ended up (completely) doing it — finished it off, often with regret or relief" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-아/어 버렸어요 (-a/eo beoryeosseoyo) = "ended up (completely) doing it — finished it off, often with regret or relief". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 다 먹어 버렸어요 ("I ended up eating it all"). Take the verb's -아/어 form and add 버리다, then conjugate that (먹다 → 먹어 버리다, 가다 → 가 버리다, 잊다 → 잊어 버리다). Stems with ㅏ/ㅗ take -아 버리다, others take -어 버리다; 하다 → 해 버리다. It adds the nuance of doing something fully/irreversibly — sometimes regret (oops), sometimes relief (good riddance). In fast speech 버렸어요 often becomes -아/어 버렸어 or contracts further.

entries.english: I'm worried that... / in case... (anxiety about something happening)
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ까 봐요 means "I'm worried that... / in case... (anxiety about something happening)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-(으)ㄹ까 봐요 (-(eu)lkka bwayo) means "I'm worried that... / in case... (anxiety about something happening)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 늦을까 봐요 ("I'm worried I'll be late"). Attach -ㄹ까 봐(요) to stems ending in a vowel (가다 → 갈까 봐, 오다 → 올까 봐) and -을까 봐(요) to stems ending in a consonant (늦다 → 늦을까 봐, 밀리다 → 밀릴까 봐). For a worry about the past, use -았/었을까 봐요 (놓쳤을까 봐요 = worried I missed it). Mid-sentence it becomes -(으)ㄹ까 봐(서) + a clause explaining what you do because of the worry.

Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 바쁘다고 했어요 ("He said he's busy"). For verbs, attach -ㄴ다고/-는다고 to the stem (가다 → 간다고 했어요, 먹다 → 먹는다고 했어요). For adjectives, attach -다고 directly (춥다 → 춥다고 했어요). Past tense uses -았/었다고 했어요 for both. In casual speech this contracts to -대(요): 간대요 (= 간다고 해요), 바쁘대 (= 바쁘다고 해). For nouns the form is N(이)라고 했어요.

entries.english: (someone) asked whether/if... — reporting a question someone asked
entries.shortExplanation: V-냐고 했어요 means "(someone) asked whether/if... — reporting a question someone asked" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.

entries.english: it's worth doing / good enough to / can be done (reasonably)
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 만해요 means "it's worth doing / good enough to / can be done (reasonably)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-(으)ㄹ 만해요 (-(eu)l manhaeyo) means "it's worth doing / good enough to / can be done (reasonably)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 볼 만해요 ("It's worth watching"). Attach -ㄹ 만하다 to vowel-ending stems (보다 → 볼 만하다, 가다 → 갈 만하다) and -을 만하다 to consonant-ending stems (먹다 → 먹을 만하다, 참다 → 참을 만하다). It means something is worth the effort or is tolerable/decent. Past: -(으)ㄹ 만했어요. Note 만하다 is written as one word here (different from the 'as big as' 만하다).

entries.english: (it) ended up / came to be that... — a change of state, often not fully by your own choice
entries.shortExplanation: V-게 됐어요 means "(it) ended up / came to be that... — a change of state, often not fully by your own choice" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "(it) ended up / came to be that... — a change of state, often not fully by your own choice" uses the pattern V-게 됐어요 (-ge dwaesseoyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 한국에 살게 됐어요 ("I ended up living in Korea"). Attach -게 되다 to any verb stem (알다 → 알게 되다, 살다 → 살게 되다) and report the result in the past: -게 됐어요 (a contraction of -게 되었어요). It frames the outcome as something that came about through circumstances rather than pure personal will, so it sounds humble and natural. Present/future: -게 돼요 / -게 될 거예요.

entries.english: while you're at it / since you're already doing it anyway
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄴ 김에 means "while you're at it / since you're already doing it anyway" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-(으)ㄴ 김에 (-(eu)n gime) = "while you're at it / since you're already doing it anyway". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 나온 김에 ("while I'm out anyway"). Attach -ㄴ 김에 to vowel-ending stems (나오다 → 나온 김에) and -은 김에 to consonant-ending stems (씻다 → 씻은 김에). You can also say 말이 나온 김에 (since it came up) and use the present -는 김에 for an ongoing action. It connects two clauses: 'since I already did X (anyway), I'll also do Y.' The Y clause carries the real point.

You can also say 말이 나온 김에 (since it came up) and use the present -는 김에 for an ongoing action. It connects two clauses: 'since I already did X (anyway), I'll also do Y.' The Y clause carries the real point.

entries.english: as much as / to the same degree as (N)
entries.shortExplanation: N만큼 means "as much as / to the same degree as (N)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "as much as / to the same degree as (N)" uses the pattern N만큼 (-mankeum). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 너만큼 잘하고 싶어요 ("I want to be as good as you"). Attach 만큼 directly to a noun with no spacing and no sound change (너 → 너만큼, 형 → 형만큼, 돈 → 돈만큼). It sets one thing as the yardstick: 'X is as Adj as N.' It also attaches to the modifier forms of verbs/adjectives (먹은 만큼 = as much as you ate, 노력한 만큼 = as much as you tried), but there 만큼 is spaced. As a particle on a plain noun it is the most common everyday use.

entries.english: considering it's (an) N / for an N (it's surprisingly...)
entries.shortExplanation: N치고 means "considering it's (an) N / for an N (it's surprisingly...)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: N치고 (-chigo) = "considering it's (an) N / for an N (it's surprisingly...)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 초보치고 잘하네요 ("You're good for a beginner"). Attach 치고 directly to a noun with no spacing (초보 → 초보치고, 겨울 → 겨울치고). It means 'given that it's N, it goes against what you'd expect from N.' You can add 는 → 치고는 to lean harder on the contrast. There's a second, opposite use, N치고 + negative = 'there's no N that isn't...' (한국 사람치고 김치 안 먹는 사람 없어요 = no Korean doesn't eat kimchi), so context tells the two apart.

entries.english: looks / seems (a certain way) — judging by appearance
entries.shortExplanation: A-아/어 보이다 means "looks / seems (a certain way) — judging by appearance" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: A-아/어 보이다 (-a/eo boida) means "looks / seems (a certain way) — judging by appearance" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 피곤해 보여요 ("You look tired"). Take an adjective's -아/어 form and add 보이다 (spaced): stems with ㅏ/ㅗ take -아 보이다 (좋다 → 좋아 보이다, 작다 → 작아 보이다), others take -어 보이다 (어리다 → 어려 보이다, 힘들다 → 힘들어 보이다), and 하다 adjectives → 해 보이다 (피곤하다 → 피곤해 보이다). 예쁘다 drops ㅡ → 예뻐 보이다, 바쁘다 → 바빠 보이다. It's only for things you judge by looking; for guesses from other evidence use -(으)ㄴ/는 것 같다.

entries.english: compared to / in comparison with (N)
entries.shortExplanation: N에 비해 means "compared to / in comparison with (N)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "compared to / in comparison with (N)" uses the pattern N에 비해 (-e bihae). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 작년에 비해 비싸요 ("It's expensive compared to last year"). Attach 에 비해 to a noun (작년 → 작년에 비해, 가격 → 가격에 비해). 비해 is the -아/어 form of 비하다 (to compare); you can also say the fuller 에 비해서 in speech or 에 비하여 in writing/formal speech. To compare against a verb/adjective clause, nominalize first: V-는 것에 비해 (사는 것에 비해 = compared to living...). It's the natural way to frame 'relative to N, this is more/less...'
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize two complete polite examples. Then substitute one word at a time and check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective.

entries.english: even though / despite the fact that
entries.shortExplanation: A/V-(으)ㄴ/는데도 means "even though / despite the fact that" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: A/V-(으)ㄴ/는데도 (-(eu)nde-do) = "even though / despite the fact that". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 열심히 했는데도 떨어졌어요 ("Even though I worked hard, I failed"). It's the -는데/-(으)ㄴ데 background ending plus 도 (even). For present verbs use -는데도 (먹다 → 먹는데도, 하다 → 하는데도); for adjectives use -(으)ㄴ데도 (춥다 → 추운데도, 바쁘다 → 바쁜데도); for the past (both) use -았/었는데도 (잤는데도 = even though I slept). Nouns take N인데도. It sets up 'even given X, surprisingly Y' — stronger and more emotional than plain -지만.

entries.english: only / merely (do) — nothing more than that
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 뿐이다 means "only / merely (do) — nothing more than that" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-(으)ㄹ 뿐이다 (-(eu)l ppun-ida) means "only / merely (do) — nothing more than that" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 할 뿐이에요 ("I'm just doing it (that's all)"). Attach -ㄹ 뿐이다 to vowel-ending stems (하다 → 할 뿐이다) and -을 뿐이다 to consonant-ending stems (믿다 → 믿을 뿐이다); 뿐 is spaced from the modifier. For a past 'I only did,' use -았/었을 뿐이다 (도와줬을 뿐이에요 = I only helped). After a noun it becomes N일 뿐이다. It limits the situation to exactly one thing — 'that's all there is to it,' often defensively or modestly.

entries.english: not only... (but also)
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 뿐만 아니라 means "not only... (but also)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "not only... (but also)" uses the pattern V-(으)ㄹ 뿐만 아니라 (-(eu)l ppunman anira). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 맛있을 뿐만 아니라 싸요 ("It's not only tasty but also cheap"). Attach -ㄹ 뿐만 아니라 to vowel stems (싸다 → 쌀 뿐만 아니라) and -을 뿐만 아니라 to consonant stems (좋다 → 좋을 뿐만 아니라); for past actions use -았/었을 뿐만 아니라. The handiest form is the noun one, N뿐만 아니라 (돈뿐만 아니라 = not only money), where 뿐만 attaches straight to the noun. The second clause adds something further, usually with 도 (also): 'not only A, but B too.'
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize two complete polite examples. Then substitute one word at a time and check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective.

entries.english: in order to / for the sake of (doing)
entries.shortExplanation: V-기 위해(서) means "in order to / for the sake of (doing)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-기 위해(서) (-gi wihae(seo)) = "in order to / for the sake of (doing)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 돈을 모으기 위해 알바해요 ("I work part-time to save money"). Attach -기 위해(서) to a verb stem (모으다 → 모으기 위해, 합격하다 → 합격하기 위해); 위해서 (with 서) is common in speech, 위하여 is the formal/written form. After a noun, use N을/를 위해(서) (가족 → 가족을 위해 = for my family). It marks a deliberate goal, so it sounds a touch more formal/purposeful than the casual -(으)려고; great for written goals, resolutions, and explanations.

entries.english: as long as / so long as (a condition holds)
entries.shortExplanation: V-는 한 means "as long as / so long as (a condition holds)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-는 한 (-neun han) means "as long as / so long as (a condition holds)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 내가 사는 한 ("as long as I live"). Attach -는 한 to a verb stem (살다 → 사는 한, with ㄹ dropping before ㄴ; 있다 → 있는 한). It very often appears in the negative, V-지 않는 한 (포기하지 않는 한 = as long as you don't give up), meaning 'unless.' 한 here means 'the limit/extent,' so the clause sets the boundary condition under which the main clause stays true. It's firmer and more conditional than a plain -(으)면 'if.'

entries.english: so much that... / as a result of being so... (and then something happened)
entries.shortExplanation: A/V-(으)ㄴ 나머지 means "so much that... / as a result of being so... (and then something happened)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "so much that... / as a result of being so... (and then something happened)" uses the pattern A/V-(으)ㄴ 나머지 (-(eu)n nameoji). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 놀란 나머지 소리쳤어요 ("I was so startled that I screamed"). Attach the past modifier -(으)ㄴ + 나머지 to verbs and adjectives (놀라다 → 놀란 나머지, 긴장하다 → 긴장한 나머지, 기쁘다 → 기쁜 나머지); consonant stems take -은 나머지 (참다 → 참은 나머지). It means an extreme degree of the first clause CAUSED the (usually negative or surprising) result in the second. It's a bit literary/dramatic, so it shines in storytelling, news, and vivid retellings rather than casual chit-chat.

entries.contextHint: Attach the past modifier -(으)ㄴ + 나머지 to verbs and adjectives (놀라다 → 놀란 나머지, 긴장하다 → 긴장한 나머지, 기쁘다 → 기쁜 나머지); consonant stems take -은 나머지 (참다 → 참은 나머지). It means an extreme degree of the first clause CAUSED the (usually negative or surprising) result in the second. It's a bit literary/dramatic, so it shines in storytelling, news, and vivid retellings rather than casual chit-chat.

entries.shortExplanation: V-다가 means "doing one thing and then switching mid-action (and in the middle...)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-다가 (-daga) = "doing one thing and then switching mid-action (and in the middle...)". entries.english: after finishing (and then, once that's done)
entries.shortExplanation: V-고 나서 means "after finishing (and then, once that's done)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-고 나서 (-go naseo) means "after finishing (and then, once that's done)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 밥 먹고 나서 ("after eating"). Attach -고 나서 to any verb stem with no sound change (먹다 → 먹고 나서, 끝나다 → 끝나고 나서, 운동하다 → 운동하고 나서). It stresses that the first action is fully completed before the second begins — stronger than plain -고. You can also say -고 나면 (once you've done X, then...) for a conditional version. Only the second clause carries the tense.

entries.english: while still in that state / leaving it as it is (without changing it)
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄴ 채로 means "while still in that state / leaving it as it is (without changing it)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "while still in that state / leaving it as it is (without changing it)" uses the pattern V-(으)ㄴ 채로 (-(eu)n chaero). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 불 켠 채로 잤어요 ("I slept with the light left on"). Attach -ㄴ 채로 to vowel-ending stems (켜다 → 켠 채로, 신다 is consonant so 신은 채로) and -은 채로 to consonant-ending stems (입다 → 입은 채로, 앉다 → 앉은 채로). It describes doing something while a prior state is left unchanged — e.g. fell asleep with the lights on. The 로 is often dropped to just -(으)ㄴ 채. It pairs with verbs that leave a lasting state (켜다, 신다, 앉다, 누르다), not ongoing actions.

entries.english: because of (an unexpected, usually bad thing that messed things up)
entries.shortExplanation: V-는 바람에 means "because of (an unexpected, usually bad thing that messed things up)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-는 바람에 (-neun barame) = "because of (an unexpected, usually bad thing that messed things up)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 늦잠 자는 바람에 ("because I overslept"). Attach -는 바람에 to any verb stem (늦다 → 늦는 바람에, 놓치다 → 놓치는 바람에, 막히다 → 막히는 바람에). Despite the -는 (present-looking) form, it always refers to a past cause, and the result clause is in the past tense. It gives a sudden, unintended reason that led to a negative or surprising outcome, so it often sounds like an excuse. It does not take adjectives.

entries.english: it's probably the case that... (but) / I'd guess... so (worry or contrast)
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 텐데 means "it's probably the case that... (but) / I'd guess... so (worry or contrast)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-(으)ㄹ 텐데 (-(eu)l tende) means "it's probably the case that... (but) / I'd guess... so (worry or contrast)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 바쁠 텐데 ("you must be busy, but..."). Attach -ㄹ 텐데 to vowel-ending stems (오다 → 올 텐데, 바쁘다 → 바쁠 텐데) and -을 텐데 to consonant-ending stems (힘들다 drops ㄹ → 힘들 텐데, 좋다 → 좋을 텐데). It expresses a strong assumption ('it must/should be...') usually followed by a contrast or worry. For a past guess use -았/었을 텐데 (피곤했을 텐데 = you must've been tired). It often trails off as a soft, caring -ㄹ 텐데(요).

entries.english: (I observed X) and then... / used to..., but now... (firsthand change)
entries.shortExplanation: V-더니 means "(I observed X) and then... / used to..., but now... (firsthand change)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "(I observed X) and then... / used to..., but now... (firsthand change)" uses the pattern V-더니 (-deoni). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 그러더니 ("and then (after doing that)"). Attach -더니 directly to a verb or adjective stem (그러다 → 그러더니, 아프다 → 아프더니). It links something you personally witnessed in the past to a result or change that followed — like 'he kept coughing, and then he got sick.' The subject is usually someone/something other than 'I.' For your own past habit leading to a present result, use -았/었더니 (많이 먹었더니 배불러 = I ate a lot, so now I'm full).

entries.english: since / seeing as (I saw or heard X, so I did Y)
entries.shortExplanation: V-길래 means "since / seeing as (I saw or heard X, so I did Y)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-길래 (-gillae) = "since / seeing as (I saw or heard X, so I did Y)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 싸길래 샀어요 ("it was cheap so I bought it"). Attach -길래 directly to a verb or adjective stem (싸다 → 싸길래, 울다 → 울길래, 맛있다 → 맛있길래). It gives a reason based on something you noticed or were told, which then prompted your own action in the response clause — so the second clause is almost always your own choice, usually in the past. For nouns use N(이)길래. It's conversational; the more formal/written equivalent is -기에.

entries.nuance: Attach -길래 directly to a verb or adjective stem (싸다 → 싸길래, 울다 → 울길래, 맛있다 → 맛있길래). For nouns use N(이)길래. It's conversational; the more formal/written equivalent is -기에.
commonMistakes: Using -길래 when the second clause isn't your own reactive action — 'It's cheap so it sells well' is a general fact (싸서 잘 팔려요), not -길래. -길래 leads to what YOU did in response.

entries.english: (it's been some time) since... (how long since an action)
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄴ 지 means "(it's been some time) since... (how long since an action)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-(으)ㄴ 지 (-(eu)n ji) means "(it's been some time) since... (how long since an action)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 온 지 얼마 안 됐어요 ("it hasn't been long since I came"). Attach -ㄴ 지 to vowel-ending stems (오다 → 온 지, 만나다 → 만난 지) and -은 지 to consonant-ending stems (먹다 → 먹은 지, 살다 drops ㄹ → 산 지). It measures elapsed time since an action and is followed by a duration plus 됐어요/지났어요 (한국에 온 지 1년 됐어요). Write 지 with a space — this time 지 is different from the negative -지 (안). 얼마나 됐어요? asks 'how long has it been?'

entries.english: even if / even though (hypothetically, no matter what)
entries.shortExplanation: V-더라도 means "even if / even though (hypothetically, no matter what)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-더라도 (-deorado) = "even if / even though (hypothetically, no matter what)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 힘들더라도 ("even if it's hard"). Attach -더라도 directly to a verb or adjective stem (가다 → 가더라도, 힘들다 → 힘들더라도, 늦다 → 늦더라도). It concedes a strong or even unlikely hypothetical — stronger than -아도/어도 — meaning 'even supposing that happens, the result still holds.' For a past supposition use -았/었더라도 (알았더라도 = even if I'd known). For nouns: N(이)더라도. It often pairs with 아무리 (no matter how) up front.

entries.english: have no choice but to / can't help but (it's the only option)
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 means "have no choice but to / can't help but (it's the only option)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 (-(eu)l subakke eopda) means "have no choice but to / can't help but (it's the only option)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 기다릴 수밖에 없어요 ("I have no choice but to wait"). Attach -ㄹ 수밖에 없다 to vowel-ending stems (가다 → 갈 수밖에 없다) and -을 수밖에 없다 to consonant-ending stems (먹다 → 먹을 수밖에 없다); ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ (살다 → 살 수밖에 없다). 밖에 means 'except,' so literally 'there is nothing except doing it.' With adjectives it means 'can't help being ~' (비싸다 → 비쌀 수밖에 없다 = it's bound to be expensive). Past: -(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없었어요.

entries.english: it's basically / it amounts to / you could say (when you do the math)
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄴ/는 셈이다 means "it's basically / it amounts to / you could say (when you do the math)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-(으)ㄴ/는 셈이다 (-(eu)n/neun semida) = "it's basically / it amounts to / you could say (when you do the math)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 거의 다 한 셈이에요 ("It's basically all done"). 셈 means a 'count/reckoning,' so this frames a situation as 'effectively the same as.' Present verbs take -는 셈이다 (사는 → 사는 셈이다), past verbs take -(으)ㄴ 셈이다 (끝난 → 끝난 셈이다), and adjectives take -(으)ㄴ 셈이다 (싼 → 싼 셈이다). It's used when reality isn't literally X but practically counts as X. Often paired with 거의 (almost) or 다 (all).
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize two complete polite examples. Then substitute one word at a time and check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective.

entries.english: might / may / it's possible that (I'm not sure)
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ지도 모르다 means "might / may / it's possible that (I'm not sure)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-(으)ㄹ지도 모르다 (-(eu)ljido moreuda) means "might / may / it's possible that (I'm not sure)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 비 올지도 몰라요 ("It might rain"). Attach -ㄹ지도 모르다 to vowel-ending stems (오다 → 올지도 모르다) and -을지도 모르다 to consonant-ending stems (늦다 → 늦을지도 모르다). It literally means 'I don't even know whether ~,' i.e. there's a real chance. For the past, use -았/었을지도 몰라요 (갔을지도 몰라요 = might have gone). The 도 can be dropped for a slightly stronger guess: -(으)ㄹ지 몰라요.

entries.english: is bound to / naturally tends to (it's only natural that)
entries.shortExplanation: V-기 마련이다 means "is bound to / naturally tends to (it's only natural that)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "is bound to / naturally tends to (it's only natural that)" uses the pattern V-기 마련이다 (-gi maryeonida). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 사람은 누구나 실수하기 마련이에요 ("Everyone is bound to make mistakes"). Attach -기 마련이다 directly to any verb or adjective stem with no sound change (늙다 → 늙기 마련이다, 바쁘다 → 바쁘기 마련이다, 실수하다 → 실수하기 마련이다). It states a general truth — something that inevitably happens by nature. A very common equivalent is -게 마련이다 (실수하게 마련이다), which means the same thing. It's used for life truths and proverb-like remarks.

entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)나 마나 means "no point doing it / whether you do it or not (the result's the same)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-(으)나 마나 (-(eu)na mana) = "no point doing it / whether you do it or not (the result's the same)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 보나 마나 뻔해요 ("It's obvious without even looking"). Attach -나 마나 to a vowel- or ㄹ-ending stem (보다 → 보나 마나) and -으나 마나 to a consonant-ending stem (먹다 → 먹으나 마나); ㄹ-stems keep ㄹ (살다 → 사나 마나). It literally pits 'whether you do (-나)' against 'whether you don't (마나, from 말다),' concluding it makes no difference. Very often it stands as a fixed adverb 보나 마나 = 'obviously / clearly.'
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize two complete polite examples. Then substitute one word at a time and check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective.

entries.english: half-heartedly / barely (do something in a half-done, distracted way)
entries.shortExplanation: V-는 둥 마는 둥 means "half-heartedly / barely (do something in a half-done, distracted way)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-는 둥 마는 둥 (-neun dung maneun dung) means "half-heartedly / barely (do something in a half-done, distracted way)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 밥을 먹는 둥 마는 둥 했어요 ("I barely picked at my food"). Attach -는 둥 마는 둥 to a verb stem (먹다 → 먹는 둥 마는 둥, 듣다 → 듣는 둥 마는 둥); ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ (놀다 → 노는 둥 마는 둥). It pairs the verb with 말다 ('not do it') to paint an action done so half-heartedly it's barely done at all. It's usually followed by 하다 or another verb describing what you did instead, often with a distracted or rushed nuance.

entries.english: also for the purpose of / partly to (doing two things at once)
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 겸 means "also for the purpose of / partly to (doing two things at once)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "also for the purpose of / partly to (doing two things at once)" uses the pattern V-(으)ㄹ 겸 (-(eu)l gyeom). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 바람도 쐴 겸 산책해요 ("I take a walk partly to get some air"). Attach -ㄹ 겸 to vowel-ending stems (보다 → 볼 겸) and -을 겸 to consonant-ending stems (먹다 → 먹을 겸); ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ (놀다 → 놀 겸). 겸 means 'combining' two aims, so you do one action to serve two purposes at once. It very often comes in pairs: A-(으)ㄹ 겸 B-(으)ㄹ 겸 (= 'partly to A, partly to B'). After it usually comes the main action.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize two complete polite examples. Then substitute one word at a time and check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective.
entries.contextHint: Attach -ㄹ 겸 to vowel-ending stems (보다 → 볼 겸) and -을 겸 to consonant-ending stems (먹다 → 먹을 겸); ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ (놀다 → 놀 겸). 겸 means 'combining' two aims, so you do one action to serve two purposes at once. It very often comes in pairs: A-(으)ㄹ 겸 B-(으)ㄹ 겸 (= 'partly to A, partly to B'). After it usually comes the main action.

It very often comes in pairs: A-(으)ㄹ 겸 B-(으)ㄹ 겸 (= 'partly to A, partly to B'). After it usually comes the main action.

It very often comes in pairs: A-(으)ㄹ 겸 B-(으)ㄹ 겸 (= 'partly to A, partly to B'). After it usually comes the main action.

겸 needs a following main action; it can't end the sentence alone like a full verb (say 볼 겸 왔어요, not just 볼 겸이에요).

entries.english: tends to be / is on the ... side (rather than strongly)
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄴ/는 편이다 means "tends to be / is on the ... side (rather than strongly)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-(으)ㄴ/는 편이다 (-(eu)n/neun pyeonida) = "tends to be / is on the ... side (rather than strongly)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 저는 매운 거 잘 먹는 편이에요 ("I'm on the side of handling spicy food well"). 편 means 'side/leaning,' so this softens a statement to 'rather' instead of 'very.' Verbs take -는 편이다 (먹다 → 먹는 편이다), adjectives take -(으)ㄴ 편이다 (크다 → 큰 편이다, 작다 → 작은 편이다). For past habits use -(으)ㄴ 편이었다. It's perfect for hedged self-description, so you sound modest rather than absolute.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize two complete polite examples. Then substitute one word at a time and check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective.
entries.contextHint: 편 means 'side/leaning,' so this softens a statement to 'rather' instead of 'very.' Verbs take -는 편이다 (먹다 → 먹는 편이다), adjectives take -(으)ㄴ 편이다 (크다 → 큰 편이다, 작다 → 작은 편이다). For past habits use -(으)ㄴ 편이었다. It's perfect for hedged self-description, so you sound modest rather than absolute.

entries.english: do (it), but... / it's true that ~, though (conceding then qualifying)
entries.shortExplanation: V-기는 하다 means "do (it), but... / it's true that ~, though (conceding then qualifying)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-기는 하다 (-gineun hada) means "do (it), but... / it's true that ~, though (conceding then qualifying)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 먹기는 했어요 ("I did eat it (but...)"). Attach -기는 하다 to a verb or adjective stem, repeating the verb's meaning in 하다 (먹다 → 먹기는 하다, 좋다 → 좋기는 하다). In speech 기는 almost always contracts to 긴 (먹긴 해요). It concedes one point while implying a 'but,' usually followed by 그런데/근데 or -지만. For other tenses, conjugate the final 하다: 먹기는 했어요 (I did eat, but...), 좋기는 할 거예요.

entries.english: as soon as
entries.shortExplanation: V자마자 means "as soon as" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V자마자 (-jamaja) = "as soon as". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 집에 오자마자 손을 씻어요. ("As soon as I get home, I wash my hands."). Add 자마자 to a verb stem to show the second action happens right after the first one finishes.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize two complete polite examples. Then substitute one word at a time and check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective.
entries.contextHint: Add 자마자 to a verb stem to show the second action happens right after the first one finishes.

patternInfo.meaning: as soon as
patternInfo.formNote: Add 자마자 to a verb stem to show the second action happens right after the first one finishes.

usagePhrases.en: As soon as I get home, I wash my hands.
As soon as I wake up, I drink water.
As soon as class ends, I go home.
As soon as I ate, I slept.

examples.en: As soon as I arrive, I call.
I knew it as soon as I saw it.
As soon as I heard, I laughed.

entries.english: if you intend to
entries.shortExplanation: V(으)려면 means "if you intend to" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V(으)려면 (-(eu)ryeomyeon) means "if you intend to" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 한국어를 잘하려면 매일 연습해요. ("If you intend to be good at Korean, practice daily."). Add 려면 after a vowel stem or 으려면 after a consonant stem to mean if you plan to do something.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize two complete polite examples. Then substitute one word at a time and check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective.
entries.contextHint: Add 려면 after a vowel stem or 으려면 after a consonant stem to mean if you plan to do something.

patternInfo.meaning: if you intend to
patternInfo.formNote: Add 려면 after a vowel stem or 으려면 after a consonant stem to mean if you plan to do something.

usagePhrases.en: If you intend to be good at Korean, practice daily.
If you want to be healthy, you must sleep well.
If you intend to read, you need glasses.
If you intend to catch the train, hurry.

examples.en: If you intend to lose weight, exercise.
If you intend to succeed, you must try.
If you intend to buy a house, save money.

entries.nuance: Add 려면 after a vowel stem or 으려면 after a consonant stem to mean if you plan to do something.
commonMistakes: Do not forget 으 after consonant stems.
Do not say the study symbol V or N out loud; replace it with a real verb stem or noun.
Check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective before using it.
